docs.title: Logging & Redirection in EOAP
docs.text:
Earth Observation Application Packages (EOAPs) describe processing tools and workflows that may run locally or on remote execution platforms. Clear logging helps developers diagnose failures and lets users follow long processing jobs.

This guide explains how to keep logs visible while producing usable data outputs with Common Workflow Language (CWL). The repository supplies three runnable tools under examples/ and includes their source definitions in the guide.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Getting started: install a runner and execute your first tool.
  • Worked logging example: compare explicit files, captured data, and captured diagnostics.
  • CWL patterns: inspect the tool definitions and output contracts.
  • Shell redirection: understand pipelines, duplication, and exit status.
  • Troubleshooting: investigate missing logs and incorrect outputs.

docs.title: How the pieces fit together
docs.text:
flowchart LR Tool[Command] -->|stdout and stderr| Runner[CWL runner] Runner -->|logging policy| Platform[Platform log collection] Platform --> View[User log view] Tool -->|explicit files or captured data| Files[Output files] Files --> Binding[CWL output collection] Binding --> Products[Returned data products]

The runner can redirect a stream into an output file before it reaches platform collection. Local execution makes diagnostics available through the runner's terminal handling; remote display and retention depend on the deployment.

docs.title: Streams, files, and execution status
docs.text:
A process has two standard output streams:

Channel Typical purpose Example stdout (file descriptor 1) Normal output, including data when the CLI uses it that way CSV rows or progress messages stderr (file descriptor 2) Diagnostics and operational messages Warnings, progress, error details Explicit output files Durable data products collected by the workflow GeoJSON, a raster, or report.json Exit status Whether the command succeeded Zero for success; nonzero for failure by default

The meaning of a stream comes from the CLI's contract. When stdout carries machine-readable data, send diagnostics to stderr so they do not corrupt that data. Writing an error message does not itself mark a job as failed: the command must also return an appropriate exit status.

docs.title: Keep logs available to the platform
docs.text:
Avoid redirecting diagnostic streams exclusively to files inside a tool. Omitting CWL's stdout and stderr fields leaves their handling to the runner. This lets an execution environment collect them according to its logging policy; it does not guarantee live streaming, retention, or access through an API.

Kubernetes normally collects container standard streams. A file written inside a container needs a separate collection mechanism to appear in those logs. A CWL runner can also redirect a subprocess before its messages reach the container streams, so verify the whole path from command to runner to platform. See the Kubernetes logging architecture.

Calrissian and other workflow engines may associate messages with individual tasks. Platforms exposing OGC API Processes can choose how to expose execution logs; check the deployment's capabilities rather than assuming a particular log endpoint exists.

docs.title: Choose a pattern
docs.text:
Tool behavior Recommended approach Emits only operational messages Leave both streams available to the runner. Writes results to named files Declare those files in CWL outputs; keep diagnostics on standard streams. Emits a data product on stdout Capture stdout as a declared file and keep diagnostics on stderr. Emits a formal diagnostic artifact on stderr Capture it deliberately and provide another route for operational visibility. Needs a persistent copy of logs Consider platform log retention or an explicit duplication strategy; check failure behavior.

Capturing a stream is appropriate when it is part of the tool's output contract. The mistake is treating every log stream as a data product without considering how users will see failures.

docs.title: What this guide includes
docs.text:
• CWL patterns: complete tools for explicit files and captured data streams, plus an example of hidden logs.
  • Shell redirection: redirection order, pipelines, tee, and exit status.
  • Troubleshooting: investigate missing logs, malformed outputs, and failures that appear successful.

The examples use small shell commands to demonstrate stream handling. Real EOAP tools should also declare their runtime dependencies, resource requirements, and inputs as appropriate.

docs.title: Specification reference
docs.text: CWL's command execution and output binding rules define how streams are captured and files are collected. See the CWL v1.2 Command Line Tool specification for the full execution model.

docs.title: CWL patterns for logs and outputs
docs.text: These complete CWL v1.2 tools have no inputs. The definitions below are included directly from the checked-in files under examples/, so the guide and runnable tools share one source. They require Bash on the execution host; they do not declare a container image.

docs.title: Write a data file and keep logs visible
docs.text:
Source: examples/explicit-file.cwl:

cwlVersion: v1.2
class: CommandLineTool
baseCommand: [bash, run.sh]
requirements:
  InitialWorkDirRequirement:
    listing:
      - entryname: run.sh
        entry: |
          #!/usr/bin/env bash
          set -euo pipefail
          printf '%s\n' 'Starting processing' >&2
          printf '%s\n' '{"status":"complete","items":3}' > report.json
          printf '%s\n' 'Report written' >&2
inputs: []
outputs:
  report:
    type: File
    outputBinding:
      glob: report.json

The command writes JSON directly to report.json. CWL collects the file through glob; the output declaration does not create it. Both progress messages remain on stderr, where the runner can handle them as logs.

There is no need for stdout: report.json here. Adding it would capture unrelated standard output into the same filename used by the script.

docs.title: Capture stdout when it is the data product
docs.text:
Source: examples/stdout-data.cwl:

cwlVersion: v1.2
class: CommandLineTool
baseCommand: [bash, run.sh]
stdout: result.csv
requirements:
  InitialWorkDirRequirement:
    listing:
      - entryname: run.sh
        entry: |
          #!/usr/bin/env bash
          set -euo pipefail
          printf '%s\n' 'Generating CSV' >&2
          printf '%s\n' 'id,value' '1,42' '2,84'
          printf '%s\n' 'CSV complete' >&2
inputs: []
outputs:
  result:
    type: File
    outputBinding:
      glob: result.csv

Here the CSV belongs on stdout, so CWL redirects that stream to result.csv. Diagnostics remain on stderr. Do not merge stderr into stdout: a progress message would become an invalid CSV row.

CWL also supports the output shortcut type: stdout. The explicit filename and File binding above make the capture destination visible to readers.

docs.title: Recognize a pattern that hides diagnostics
docs.text:
Source: examples/captured-logs.cwl. Run it to compare its behavior:

cwlVersion: v1.2
class: CommandLineTool
baseCommand: [bash, run.sh]
stdout: result.txt
stderr: errors.txt
requirements:
  InitialWorkDirRequirement:
    listing:
      - entryname: run.sh
        entry: |
          #!/usr/bin/env bash
          printf '%s\n' 'Starting processing'
          printf '%s\n' 'Warning: demonstration only' >&2
inputs: []
outputs:
  result:
    type: File
    outputBinding:
      glob: result.txt
  errors:
    type: File
    outputBinding:
      glob: errors.txt

Both messages go to files rather than remaining on the command's standard streams. The filenames do not make these messages data products. A runner may expose the files separately, but platform stream collection cannot be assumed to show their contents.

If this tool fails, do not assume its declared log artifacts will still be published. Failure handling and access to working directories depend on the runner and deployment.

docs.title: Validate and compare locally
docs.text:
Install cwltool in a Python virtual environment, then validate the checked-in examples from the repository root:

python -m pip install cwltool
cwltool --validate examples/explicit-file.cwl
cwltool --validate examples/stdout-data.cwl
cwltool --validate examples/captured-logs.cwl

Run each tool with a separate output directory:

cwltool --outdir out/explicit examples/explicit-file.cwl
cwltool --outdir out/csv examples/stdout-data.cwl
cwltool --outdir out/captured examples/captured-logs.cwl

Check that:

  • out/explicit/report.json contains JSON and no progress messages.
  • out/csv/result.csv contains only the header and two data rows.
  • The first two tools expose diagnostics through the runner's log handling.
  • The third tool puts its messages in result.txt and errors.txt.

The runner's own final output description is separate from the tool's captured stream. Do not confuse cwltool's output JSON with report.json or result.csv.

docs.title: Failure is part of the contract
docs.text:
By default, CWL treats exit code zero as success. A diagnostic printed to stderr can be a warning from a successful command; it is not a failure signal by itself. Return nonzero for failures and use CWL's successCodes, temporaryFailCodes, or permanentFailCodes only when the underlying CLI's exit-code contract requires them.

A required output file must also exist for output collection to succeed. Avoid producing a success-shaped placeholder after processing fails.

See the CWL specification for stdout, stderr, output bindings, and exit-code handling.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Run a small tool locally to see how diagnostics and a data product travel through a CWL runner. These examples require Python 3, a virtual environment, and Bash. They have no container requirements, external data inputs, or processing-library dependencies. Installing the Python tools requires network access.

docs.title: Prepare the environment
docs.text:
Clone the repository and enter its root:

git clone https://github.com/eoap/logging-and-redirection.git
cd logging-and-redirection
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install cwltool

On Windows, use an environment with Bash available, such as WSL, for these tools. The commands above assume a Unix shell.

Check the runner and shell:

cwltool --version
bash --version

cwltool is unpinned here. Record its version when comparing results across environments.

docs.title: Validate and run a first tool
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cwltool --validate examples/explicit-file.cwl
cwltool --outdir out/explicit examples/explicit-file.cwl

Expect the diagnostic messages Starting processing and Report written in the terminal, alongside runner messages. The tool creates out/explicit/report.json:

{"status":"complete","items":3}

Inspect the file:

cat out/explicit/report.json

The runner also prints a CWL output description containing information about the collected file. That description is separate from the JSON data inside report.json.

docs.title: Understand the result
docs.text:
The tool writes the report explicitly and leaves stderr available to the runner. Its output binding collects the report after execution. This separates data collection from progress reporting.

Local terminal visibility does not establish how a remote platform displays or retains logs. Repeat a representative run in the target environment and check its task logging interface.

Continue with the worked comparison to contrast this behavior with captured stdout and captured diagnostics. See troubleshooting if execution fails.

docs.title: Worked logging example
docs.text:
The three tools under examples/ isolate different stream contracts. They use tiny synthetic outputs so you can inspect the difference without downloading satellite data or container images.

Run the commands from the repository root after completing getting started. Their definitions and explanations appear in CWL patterns.

docs.title: Compare the tools
docs.text: Tool Data destination Diagnostic destination Expected result examples/explicit-file.cwl Explicit report.json file stderr, handled by the runner JSON report and visible progress examples/stdout-data.cwl stdout captured as result.csv stderr, handled by the runner Clean CSV and visible progress examples/captured-logs.cwl No processing data product stdout and stderr captured into files Messages in artifacts rather than the command's live streams

docs.title: Explicit file output
docs.text:
cwltool --outdir out/explicit examples/explicit-file.cwl
cat out/explicit/report.json

The report contains the status and item count. Starting processing and Report written are diagnostics, so the script sends them to stderr. Neither appears inside the report.

docs.title: Stdout as data
docs.text:
cwltool --outdir out/csv examples/stdout-data.cwl
cat out/csv/result.csv

Expected file contents:

id,value
1,42
2,84

The messages Generating CSV and CSV complete remain on stderr. Capturing stdout is correct because the CLI's stdout is the data product. Merging stderr into stdout would corrupt this contract.

docs.title: Captured diagnostics
docs.text:
cwltool --outdir out/captured examples/captured-logs.cwl
cat out/captured/result.txt
cat out/captured/errors.txt

result.txt contains Starting processing; errors.txt contains Warning: demonstration only. Both are logs, despite being declared as file outputs. Runner status messages may still appear in the terminal, and a runner may choose to display captured logs, but the command no longer leaves these messages on its original streams.

This is an intentional demonstration of a problematic logging pattern. Both messages are produced by a successful command: the warning does not cause the example to fail.

docs.title: What this comparison establishes
docs.text:
These runs demonstrate tool-level stream destinations and output collection on your local runner. They do not establish remote log retention, access through an OGC API Processes service, or retrieval of captured files after failed jobs.

For deployment, also exercise a controlled failure and confirm that the platform reports failure and exposes the diagnostics you need. Use the troubleshooting checklist to investigate gaps.

docs.title: Shell redirection and pipelines
docs.text:
A CWL tool can preserve standard streams in its definition and still hide them inside a shell script. Inspect both layers when reviewing an application package.

The examples on this page use Bash. Ordinary CWL baseCommand and arguments are command arguments, not shell syntax: a literal > does not become a redirection unless a shell interprets it. An explicit script, as used in the CWL examples, makes that behavior easier to inspect.

docs.title: Understand the destination
docs.text:
Bash syntax Effect command > result.txt Replace result.txt with stdout from the command. command >> result.txt Append stdout to the file. command 2> errors.txt Write stderr to a file. command > combined.log 2>&1 Send stdout and stderr to the same file. command > /dev/null 2>&1 Discard both streams. printf '%s\n' 'Processing' >&2 Send a message to stderr.

Use file redirection deliberately for data products. Avoid blanket suppression or capture of diagnostics in production wrappers unless another mechanism provides the required visibility.

docs.title: Redirection order matters
docs.text:
Bash processes redirections from left to right:

command > combined.log 2>&1

First stdout is pointed at the file, then stderr is pointed at stdout's current destination. Both streams reach the file.

command 2>&1 > result.txt

Here stderr is first pointed at stdout's original destination. Only stdout is subsequently moved to the file. The two forms have different behavior.

docs.title: Duplicate diagnostics with tee
docs.text:
If an application needs a file copy and visible diagnostics, tee can duplicate a stream. For a command whose stdout and stderr are both human-readable logs:

set -o pipefail
command 2>&1 | tee processing.log

This merges the two streams and writes their combined contents both to processing.log and to the pipeline's stdout. It loses the distinction between stdout and stderr. Do not use this pattern when stdout contains CSV, JSON, or another data product.

tee does not bypass CWL redirection. If the enclosing CWL tool captures stdout, the duplicated messages still go to that capture destination. Also decide whether the log file needs to be declared as an output and how failed-run logs will be retained.

docs.title: Preserve failure through pipelines
docs.text:
Without pipefail, Bash normally reports the exit status of the last command in a pipeline. A failed processor followed by a successful tee can therefore appear successful.

Try this small demonstration:

bash -c 'exit 7' | tee demonstration.log

Then repeat with pipeline failure propagation enabled:

set -o pipefail
bash -c 'exit 7' | tee demonstration.log

With pipefail, a failing pipeline returns the status of its rightmost failing command. In a script, handle that nonzero result or let an appropriate error policy stop execution. set -euo pipefail is a useful starting point for simple Bash wrappers, but -e has exceptions in conditionals and other contexts; review the actual control flow rather than treating it as a complete error-handling strategy.

docs.title: Buffering can delay visible messages
docs.text:
A process may buffer output differently when writing to a pipe or file instead of a terminal. Missing immediate progress does not necessarily mean messages were redirected away. Use the application's flushing or unbuffered-output options when available, and test with the same runner and container setup used in deployment.

For shell semantics, consult the GNU Bash manual, especially its sections on redirections, pipelines, and the set builtin.

docs.title: Troubleshooting logging and outputs
docs.text: Investigate the command, the CWL runner, and the execution platform separately. A local run confirms tool behavior, while a deployed run confirms collection, access, and retention in the target environment.

docs.title: Logs are missing
docs.text:
1. Check whether the application emitted messages at all. Run a small representative job locally and inspect stdout, stderr, and its exit status.
  2. Inspect the CWL tool for stdout and stderr capture fields.
  3. Inspect scripts and wrappers for >, 2>, 2>&1, /dev/null, or application options that write logs only to a file.
  4. Determine how the runner routes subprocess streams. Messages may be available in runner logs even when they do not appear in the expected task view.
  5. Check the target platform's task or container selection, access permissions, collection configuration, and retention period.

If logs were intentionally captured as files, find out whether the runner retains those files after failures. Declaring a CWL output alone does not establish a failed-job log retrieval policy.

docs.title: Logs arrive late
docs.text: Check application buffering and whether the platform batches messages before displaying them. Test a command that emits periodic messages with explicit flushing to distinguish application buffering from collection delay. Avoid changing the data-output format just to make progress visible.

docs.title: JSON or CSV contains log messages
docs.text:
Inspect the CLI's stdout contract. Look for diagnostics printed to stdout and wrappers that merge stderr into stdout.

Send progress and diagnostics to stderr when stdout is reserved for data, or write the result to an explicit file. Check the captured product with a parser; a filename extension does not prove the contents are valid.

docs.title: A failed command appears successful
docs.text:
Check the command's exit code, shell conditionals, pipelines, and CWL exit-code overrides. A wrapper may print an error and then return zero, or a successful tee may hide an earlier failure when pipefail is disabled.

Add a deliberate failure during testing and verify that the runner marks the job as failed. Confirm that useful diagnostic messages remain accessible for that failed run.

docs.title: An expected output is missing
docs.text:
Confirm that the command creates the file in the working directory and that the CWL glob matches its name. Keep progress messages separate from data generation so a redirected message cannot accidentally create a misleading output artifact.

Inspect the original processing error before assuming output binding is the root cause. A missing file can be a consequence of an earlier failure.

docs.title: Review before deployment
docs.text:
Check Evidence to collect Stream contract Identify which streams contain data and which contain diagnostics. Successful execution Parse the output product and confirm required files exist. Failed execution Trigger a controlled failure and confirm the job fails with accessible diagnostics. Pipeline behavior Verify a failed upstream command is not masked by a later command. Remote visibility Find messages for the correct job and task on the target platform. Retention Establish how long logs and failed-job artifacts remain accessible. Message content Include useful task context without printing credentials or sensitive inputs.

For concurrent workflows, use task identifiers and timestamps when practical. Logs from separate streams or tasks may be interleaved; do not rely on display order alone to reconstruct causality.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:

  • Kubernetes logging architecture: container streams and cluster logging mechanisms.
  • GNU Bash manual: shell redirection and pipeline behavior.
